questions.title: How does the partition function $Z(x)$ cancel out in the DPO derivation?
questions.question_body:
I am reading the 'Direct Preference Optimization' paper and trying to follow the derivation in Section 3. The authors define the optimal policy as $\pi_r(y\mid x) = \frac{1}{Z(x)}\pi_\text{ref}(y\mid x)\exp\left(\frac{1}{\beta}r(x, y)\right)$ and then rearrange it to solve for the reward: $r(x,y) =\beta \log \frac{\pi_r(y\mid x)}{\pi_\text{ref}(y\mid x)} + \beta \log Z(x)$. 

When they substitute this into the Bradley-Terry model probability $p^*(y_1\succ y_2 \mid x)=\sigma(r^*(x, y_1) - r^*(x, y_2))$, they claim the partition function cancels out. Since $Z(x)$ depends on the prompt $x$, doesn't it remain in the equation? Could someone walk through the algebraic steps showing exactly how $\beta \log Z(x)$ disappears when taking the difference between two rewards for the same prompt?

questions.title: What is the intuitive role of the sigmoid weighting term in the DPO gradient?
questions.question_body:
In Section 3, under 'What does the DPO update do?', the paper presents the gradient of the DPO loss:
$$ \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_\text{DPO} \propto -\sigma(\hat{r}_\theta(x, y_l) - \hat{r}_\theta (x, y_w)) [\nabla_\theta\log \pi(y_w \mid x) - \nabla_\theta\log\pi(y_l \mid x)] $$
The paper states that this sigmoid term acts as a dynamic importance weight that prevents model degeneration. 

If I understand correctly, $\hat{r}_\theta$ is the implicit reward. If the model already ranks the preferred response $y_w$ much higher than the dispreferred $y_l$, then $\hat{r}_\theta(x, y_l) - \hat{r}_\\theta (x, y_w)$ will be a large negative number, making the sigmoid close to 0. Does this mean DPO effectively stops updating once the model gets the ranking right? Conversely, if the model mistakenly thinks $y_l$ is better, does the weight approach 1? How is this different from a standard unlikelihood loss which just pushes down $y_l$ regardless of its current score relative to $y_w$?

questions.title: Clarification on Reference Policy Initialization when SFT Model is Unavailable
questions.question_body:
The 'DPO outline' subsection mentions that ideally $\pi_\text{ref}$ is initialized as the Supervised Fine-Tuned (SFT) model ($\pi^\text{SFT}$). However, it also says: 'when $\pi^\text{SFT}$ is not available, we initialize $\pi_\\text{ref}$ by maximizing likelihood of preferred completions'. 

In the Single-Turn Dialogue experiment (Section 5.3), they mention no pre-trained SFT model was available, so they trained a reference model on preferred completions. My confusion is: if we train $\\pi_\\text{ref}$ only on the *chosen* responses ($y_w$), isn't this effectively doing Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)? If so, why distinguish it from an SFT model? Is there a subtle difference in how this reference model is used during DPO training versus how a standard SFT model serves as a starting point for PPO? Does initializing $\\pi_\\text{ref}$ this way introduce bias since it has never seen the rejected responses $y_l$?

questions.title: Does DPO restrict the space of learnable reward functions compared to explicit Reward Modeling?
questions.question_body:
In Section 4 ('Theoretical Analysis'), Theorem 1 claims that 'all reward classes consistent with... Bradley-Terry models can be represented with the reparameterization $r(x, y) = \beta \log \frac{\\pi(y\\mid x)}{\\pi_\\text{ref}(y\\mid x)}$'. 

The proof involves a projection operator $f$ that normalizes the reward by subtracting $\\beta\\log Z(x)$. The authors argue this selects a specific representative from an equivalence class of reward functions (where two rewards are equivalent if they differ only by a function of $x$). 

My question is: In standard RLHF with an explicit reward model $r_\\phi$, do we ever care about recovering the 'true' absolute values of the reward function, or only the relative ordering? If standard RLHF also only cares about relative ordering (since PPO optimizes based on advantage estimates), does DPO actually lose any expressivity? Or are there cases where an explicit reward model could learn a function outside this specific parameterization that would lead to a better policy?

questions.title: Why does PPO seem less robust to sampling temperature than DPO in experiments?
questions.question_body:
Looking at Figure 2 (referenced in Section 5.2 regarding Summarization), the text notes that 'DPO is much more robust to sampling temperature than PPO,' and that PPO performance degrades significantly at high temperatures while DPO remains stable. 

Since both methods ostensibly optimize similar objectives (maximizing reward subject to a KL constraint), why would their behavior diverge so drastically during inference with different temperatures? Is this because PPO tends to overfit to high-reward modes during training (mode collapse), making it brittle when stochasticity is introduced at test time? Or does the direct optimization of probabilities in DPO preserve more entropy in policy outputs naturally? The paper mentions PPO requires careful hyperparameter tuning; could this instability be purely a result of suboptimal tuning in their setup?

questions.title: Understanding Equivalence Classes: Why add/subtract a function of x?
questions.question_body:
Definition 1 in Section 4 defines two reward functions as equivalent if $r(x, y)-r'(x, y) = f(x)$ for some function $f$. I understand mathematically why this works for Bradley-Terry (since it uses differences), but conceptually I'm stuck.

If I have a reward function that assigns +10 to good answers and -10 to bad ones for Prompt A, and another function assigning +5 and -5 for Prompt A (but keeping differences constant), these are equivalent under Definition 1 where f(A)=5. But what if I shift rewards differently for different prompts? E.g., adding 5 for Prompt A but adding 20 for Prompt B?

Does Lemma 1 imply that human preference data fundamentally cannot distinguish between these shifted versions? And if so, why does standard Reward Modeling usually try to predict absolute scores rather than just relative margins? Is it just convention or convenience?
